grammar noun

also grammatical, grammar book, rules of grammar

grammatica, grammaticae f.

noun, first declension · Declension on Wiktionary

grammar; the study of language and of the poets

One of the Greek words that Cicero says use has made Latin (Fin. 3.5). Roman grammar took in more than rules: Quintilian divides it into correct speech and the explanation of the poets (1.4.2). Grammatical is grammaticus; according to the rules, grammaticē (Quint. 1.6.27).

Other words

  • grammaticē, grammaticēs f. — grammar (the Greek form)

    noun · also used · classical · Quint. 1.4.2; 1.5.1 (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    Quintilian’s form of the word, declined in Greek.

  • ars grammatica — grammar; a grammar book

    also used · classical · Quint. 1.5.54 (Lewis & Short, s.v. grammaticus); Traupman 246; Traupman 323

    Ars alone is a grammar book, like Donatus’s Ars; Traupman gives ars for a textbook (p. 32).

  • litterātūra, litterātūrae f. — grammar, the first teaching of letters

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Quint. 2.1.4: grammaticē (quam in Latīnum trānsferentēs litterātūram vocāvērunt); Sen. Ep. 88.20 (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    The Latin rendering of grammaticē, from litterae; in Seneca the first teaching of letters to children. In modern Latin it is literature.

Examples

  • haec igitur professiō, cum brevissimē in duās partēs dīvidātur, rēctē loquendī scientiam et poētārum ēnarrātiōnem, plūs habet in recessū quam fronte prōmittit

    This profession, then, though in the briefest terms it divides into two parts, the science of speaking correctly and the explanation of the poets, has more behind it than it shows in frontQuint. 1.4.2

  • aliud esse Latīnē aliud grammaticē loquī

    speaking Latin is one thing, speaking grammar anotherQuint. 1.6.27
